original_question: Let B^(H): L2(0,1) -> l2 be the Hausdorff moment operator defined by [B^(H) z]_j = integral_0^1 t^(j-1) z(t) dt for j = 1, 2, .... The inverse problem B^(H) z = y is known to be ill-posed of type I, and there exists an infinite-dimensional subspace of the data space l2 on which the inverse of B^(H) is continuous. Which infinite-dimensional subspace is it?
target_in_paper: Open Question 1 in Section 1 (Introduction): "What is the infinite dimensional subspace of ell^2, on which the inverse of the operator B^(H) is continuous?"
correct_elements: Your draft targets the correct part of the paper almost exactly: it uses the same Hausdorff moment operator B^(H): L^2(0,1) -> ell^2, the same inverse problem B^(H) z = y, the same observation that the problem is ill-posed of type I, and the same focus on the infinite-dimensional data subspace on which the inverse is continuous. That is precisely the content of Open Question 1.
missing_details: The paper poses this as an open characterization problem, not as a subspace that has already been explicitly identified.
The inverse should be understood as the restricted inverse on a subspace Y_1 of the data space lying inside the range R(B^(H)); otherwise B^(H)^(-1) is not defined.
To be faithful to type-I ill-posedness in the sense of Nashed, the relevant subspace should be taken infinite-dimensional and closed.
Continuity should be stated quantitatively: there should exist a constant C > 0 such that ||B^(H)^(-1) y||_{L^2(0,1)} <= C ||y||_{ell^2} for all y in Y_1.
Because B^(H) is injective, the inverse should be written as the restricted inverse B^(H)^(-1): Y_1 -> L^2(0,1).
For a fully stand-alone formulation, the ambient spaces and norms should be made explicit; the paper works in the real Hilbert spaces L^2(0,1) and ell^2.
If one wants paper-faithful wording, the task is to characterize the stable subspace rather than to ask for a single named or canonical subspace.
refined_question: Let B^(H): L^2(0,1) -> ell^2 be the Hausdorff moment operator defined by [B^(H) z]_j = integral_0^1 t^(j-1) z(t) dt for j = 1,2,.... It is known that B^(H) is injective, bounded, non-compact, and has non-closed range, so the inverse problem B^(H) z = y is ill-posed of type I in the sense of Nashed. Characterize explicitly an infinite-dimensional closed subspace Y_1 of R(B^(H)) contained in ell^2 such that the restricted inverse B^(H)^(-1): Y_1 -> L^2(0,1) is continuous; equivalently, determine a subspace Y_1 and a constant C > 0 for which ||B^(H)^(-1) y||_{L^2(0,1)} <= C ||y||_{ell^2} holds for all y in Y_1.
justification: The draft is already very close to the paper's exact target: Open Question 1 in the introduction. I kept the scope on B^(H) itself and did not broaden to the composite operator A = B^(H) o J or to the later open questions. I sharpened the wording only by making explicit what continuity of the inverse means, by restricting the inverse to a subspace of the range, and by adding the closed-subspace/bounded-inverse formulation that is implicit in the type-I ill-posedness framework invoked by the paper and spelled out in the cited background paper [4].
